title: Lifestyle Inflation: 20 Ways Your Raise Disappears

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. You got the raise. Congratulations. Five thousand dollars more a year, maybe ten. And then something strange happens. A year later, your savings look exactly the same. Your stress looks exactly the same. The raise just vanished. Today, twenty ways your raise disappears, and how to keep the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Lifestyle inflation, sometimes called lifestyle creep, is when your spending rises every time your income does, so a higher salary never turns into more savings.

card.label: lifestyle inflation
card.sub: when spending rises with every raise

scenes.short_hook: Where did your raise go? Probably here.

scenes.text: Lifestyle inflation is sneaky because none of it feels like overspending. It feels like finally living at the level you've earned. A slightly nicer apartment. A newer car. Better groceries. More dinners out. Each upgrade is small and reasonable. Together, they can swallow an entire raise, and then some.
scenes.caption: IT FEELS EARNED

scenes.text: We'll look at it from three angles. Angle one, the numbers: the first seven leaks, where the money from a raise actually goes. Angle two, the psychology: why upgrades feel necessary and become permanent. And angle three, the playbook: the leaks that hurt your long term wealth, and a simple rule that lets you enjoy a raise and still get richer from it.
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: And if you've ever wondered why people earning twice as much as you still say they're broke, this video answers that too. Let's start with the numbers.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Every number here comes from a named source. Spending patterns come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Expenditure Survey, which tracks how American households spend at different income levels. Tax rules come from the IRS. Retirement plan rules come from the IRS and the Department of Labor. Examples use stated, simple math, like a seven percent average yearly return. That's an illustration, not a promise. This is education, not financial advice.
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: The Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Expenditure Survey shows a clear pattern. Households with higher incomes spend more in almost every category, from housing to food away from home to entertainment.

card.label: more income
card.sub: in almost every category (BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey)

scenes.text: The phrase keeping up with the Joneses comes from a comic strip that started in nineteen thirteen. It followed a family desperately trying to match the lifestyle of their neighbors, the Joneses, who were never actually shown. That's the joke. The people we compete with are often people we barely know, and whose real finances we never see.
scenes.caption: THE JONESES, 1913

scenes.text: A century later, the Joneses aren't just next door. They're on every screen. Friends, influencers, celebrities and strangers, all showing their best moments. Economists have found that people's satisfaction with their income often depends on how it compares with others around them, not just on the amount itself. That's why a raise can feel great until you see what someone else got.
scenes.caption: THE JONESES ARE EVERYWHERE

scenes.text: The good news is that you can choose your comparison. Instead of comparing your lifestyle with other people's, compare your savings rate this year with your savings rate last year. That's a race you can actually win, and it's the only one that changes your future.
scenes.caption: COMPARE WITH LAST YEAR'S YOU

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Where does the money from a raise actually go? Let's follow a five thousand dollar raise.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Leak number one. Taxes take the first bite.

card.title: Taxes take the first bite
card.sub: the raise is smaller than it looks

scenes.caption: LEAK 1

scenes.text: A five thousand dollar raise is not five thousand dollars in your pocket. Federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare, and in many places state income tax all come out first. Depending on your situation, the take home part of a five thousand dollar raise might be closer to thirty five hundred or four thousand dollars. That's around three hundred dollars a month.
scenes.caption: $5,000 BECOMES ~$300 A MONTH

scenes.text: This matters because people mentally spend the full raise. They think, I make five thousand more, so I can afford a four hundred dollar car payment. But the real extra money might be three hundred a month. The upgrade is already bigger than the raise before it starts.
scenes.caption: SPENT BEFORE IT ARRIVES

scenes.text: And by the way, a common myth is that a raise can push you into a higher bracket and make you take home less. That's not how it works. In the United States, only the dollars above a bracket threshold are taxed at the higher rate. A raise almost always means more take home pay, just less than the headline number. Try this: after your next raise, look at your actual paycheck before planning anything.
scenes.caption: ONLY THE EXTRA IS TAXED MORE

scenes.text: A five thousand dollar raise, after federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare and state taxes, might add only about three hundred dollars a month to take home pay, depending on your situation.
Leak number two. The housing upgrade.

card.title: The housing upgrade
card.sub: a bigger place, a bigger everything

scenes.caption: LEAK 2

scenes.text: Housing is the biggest line in most budgets, and the most common place a raise goes. A nicer neighborhood, one more bedroom, a building with a gym. Moving up two hundred or three hundred dollars a month in rent can feel like a reasonable reward. And just like that, most of the raise is spent, every month, for as long as you live there.
scenes.caption: RENT GOES UP

scenes.text: And it's never just rent. A bigger place means more furniture, higher utilities, higher renter's insurance, maybe a parking spot. A house means higher property taxes and maintenance. The housing upgrade is usually the leak that pulls several other leaks along with it.
scenes.caption: AND EVERYTHING WITH IT

scenes.text: Try this: when your lease comes up after a raise, ask a different question. Not can I afford a nicer place? But would a nicer place make me happier than having an extra three thousand dollars a year in savings? Sometimes the answer is yes. Often, it isn't.
scenes.caption: ASK A DIFFERENT QUESTION

scenes.text: Leak number three. The car upgrade.
scenes.caption: LEAK 3

scenes.text: A raise often comes with a new car. The old one works, but it's getting older, and now you can afford the payment. Remember from my car payment video, the average new car payment has been around seven hundred fifty dollars a month in recent years. Even a modest upgrade can eat two or three hundred dollars of your monthly raise.
scenes.caption: THE NEW CAR

scenes.text: Add higher insurance for a newer, more expensive car, and the upgrade can easily cost more than the raise itself. The raise lasts as long as your job. The car payment lasts five to seven years, even if your job changes.
scenes.caption: LONGER THAN THE RAISE

scenes.text: Try this: keep your current car until it truly needs replacing, and start paying yourself a car payment now into a savings account. When the time comes, you'll buy the next car with a big down payment, or cash, and your raise will have built savings instead of a loan.
scenes.caption: PAY YOURSELF FIRST

scenes.text: Leak number four. Subscriptions.
scenes.caption: LEAK 4

scenes.text: Streaming services, music, cloud storage, apps, meal kits, fitness classes, premium memberships. Each one is ten, fifteen, or twenty dollars a month. With a raise, adding one more feels like nothing. But eight or ten subscriptions can easily reach one hundred fifty to two hundred dollars a month, which is over two thousand dollars a year.
scenes.caption: TEN DOLLARS AT A TIME

scenes.text: Subscriptions are designed to be easy to start and easy to forget. Free trials that convert automatically. Annual renewals that arrive when you're not paying attention. Price increases that happen quietly. Many people pay for services they haven't used in months.
scenes.caption: EASY TO FORGET

scenes.text: Try this: list every subscription from your bank and card statements. Cancel anything you haven't used in the last month. Rotate streaming services instead of keeping them all. One month for one service, then switch. You'll still have plenty to watch.
scenes.caption: LIST, CANCEL, ROTATE

scenes.text: Leak number five. Eating out and delivery.
scenes.caption: LEAK 5

scenes.text: When money is tight, people cook. When money loosens, takeout and restaurants become a habit. The BLS data shows food away from home rising with income. And delivery adds fees, tips and menu markups, so the same meal can cost much more than eating at the restaurant, and far more than cooking.
scenes.caption: FOOD AWAY FROM HOME

scenes.text: Eating out isn't bad. It's one of the best ways to spend time with people you love. The problem is when it replaces home cooking out of habit, not choice. A few extra delivery orders a week can add up to several hundred dollars a month.
scenes.caption: HABIT VS CHOICE

scenes.text: Try this: decide how many meals out per week fit your goals, then enjoy them fully, without guilt. For everything else, keep a few easy, fast meals at home for tired nights, which is when most delivery orders happen.
scenes.caption: PLAN THE EASY NIGHTS

scenes.text: Leak number six. Premium versions of everyday things.
scenes.caption: LEAK 6

scenes.text: This is the quietest leak. After a raise, the grocery cart changes. Organic versions, name brands, fancier coffee, nicer shampoo, better wine. None of these choices is big. But a ten to twenty percent increase on groceries and household items can add up to over one hundred dollars a month for a family.
scenes.caption: THE QUIET UPGRADE

scenes.text: Some upgrades are worth it to you, and that's fine. The leak happens when you upgrade everything automatically, without asking which ones actually matter. Many store brands are made to similar standards as name brands, at a lower price.
scenes.caption: UPGRADE WHAT MATTERS

scenes.text: Try this: pick three things where premium truly makes you happier, maybe coffee, a good mattress, quality shoes. Spend well on those. For everything else, buy the good enough version. That's how you upgrade your life without upgrading your whole budget.
scenes.caption: PICK THREE

scenes.text: Leak number seven. Constant tech upgrades.
scenes.caption: LEAK 7

scenes.text: New phones, laptops, watches, headphones and gaming gear arrive every year, and carriers make upgrading easy with monthly payment plans. A thousand dollar phone spread over two or three years looks like a small monthly charge, and the next upgrade is always being advertised.
scenes.caption: THE ANNUAL UPGRADE

scenes.text: Modern devices often last many years with a new battery and good care. Upgrading every year or two instead of every four or five can cost hundreds of dollars a year, often for features you barely notice after the first week.
scenes.caption: IT STILL WORKS

scenes.text: Try this: keep your devices until they stop doing what you need, not until a new one comes out. When you do upgrade, consider the previous year's model, which often costs much less and does almost everything the newest one does.
scenes.caption: LAST YEAR'S MODEL

scenes.text: Let's add up the first seven leaks with very modest numbers. Higher rent, two hundred. Car upgrade, two hundred. Subscriptions, fifty. More eating out, one hundred. Premium groceries, fifty. Tech, thirty. That's six hundred thirty dollars a month. Remember, the raise only added about three hundred dollars of take home pay. The lifestyle grew twice as fast as the income.
scenes.caption: $630 OF NEW SPENDING

scenes.text: A five thousand dollar raise can add about three hundred dollars a month to take home pay. Seven small upgrades can add over six hundred dollars a month in new spending.
That's how people earn more and end up with less. Now, why do these upgrades feel so necessary? Angle two.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Angle two. The psychology. Eight reasons upgrades feel necessary, and then become permanent.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Leak number eight. The hedonic treadmill.
scenes.caption: LEAK 8
scenes.short_hook: Why every upgrade becomes your new normal

scenes.text: Psychologists use the term hedonic treadmill to describe how people adapt to changes in their lives. A new apartment, a new car or a pay raise feels great at first. But within months, it becomes normal. The happiness boost fades, and we start looking for the next upgrade.
scenes.caption: NEW BECOMES NORMAL

scenes.text: This is why lifestyle inflation never feels like enough. You run faster, earn more, spend more, and your happiness stays roughly in the same place. Meanwhile, the costs stay locked in. You're running on a treadmill that keeps getting more expensive.
scenes.caption: RUNNING IN PLACE

scenes.text: Try this: before any permanent upgrade, ask, how will I feel about this in six months, when it's normal? If the honest answer is that you won't notice it much, keep the money. Spend instead on things that keep giving, like experiences, health, and time with people you love.
scenes.caption: WHAT KEEPS GIVING

scenes.text: Leak number nine. A new peer group.
scenes.caption: LEAK 9

scenes.text: Raises often come with a new role, a new company or a new circle. And new peers bring new norms. Different restaurants for lunch, more expensive hobbies, nicer vacations, bigger houses. What was a luxury in your old circle is ordinary in the new one.
scenes.caption: NEW CIRCLE, NEW NORMS

scenes.text: It's natural to want to fit in. But your new peers might have different finances. Some earn more. Some have family money. Some carry a lot of debt. Matching their lifestyle with your income is one of the fastest ways to lose a raise.
scenes.caption: THEIR NORMAL ISN'T YOUR PLAN

scenes.text: Try this: join in on your terms. Say yes to the events that matter, suggest cheaper options sometimes, and don't apologize for having goals. You'll find that many people respect someone who's clear about their priorities.
scenes.caption: JOIN ON YOUR TERMS

scenes.text: Leak number ten. Treat yourself becomes every week.
scenes.caption: LEAK 10

scenes.text: Treats are great. The problem is frequency. When a treat is rare, it's special. When it becomes weekly, it's just spending. After a raise, treats tend to multiply. The Friday dinner, the weekend shopping trip, the random online order because it was a long day.
scenes.caption: TREATS MULTIPLY

scenes.text: And the more often you treat yourself, the less each treat feels like a treat. That's the hedonic treadmill again. You need more to feel the same. Rare treats are both cheaper and more enjoyable.
scenes.caption: RARE IS BETTER

scenes.text: Try this: give yourself a set amount of fun money each month, and spend it any way you like, guilt free. When it's gone, it's gone until next month. Limits make treats feel special again.
scenes.caption: A FUN MONEY BUDGET

scenes.text: Leak number eleven. Paying for convenience.
scenes.caption: LEAK 11

scenes.text: With more income, it's tempting to pay for time. Cleaning services, delivery, rideshares, dry cleaning, grocery pickup. Some of these can genuinely be worth it, especially if they free time for family, rest or higher paying work. Research on time and happiness suggests that buying time can improve well being.
scenes.caption: BUYING TIME

scenes.text: The leak happens when convenience spending isn't a choice, it's a default. Rideshares when a short walk or bus works fine. Delivery for things you'll pass on the way home. Convenience is easy to justify one purchase at a time, and hard to see in total.
scenes.caption: CONVENIENCE BY DEFAULT

scenes.text: Try this: choose one or two convenience services that genuinely give you meaningful time, and keep them. Drop the rest. That way you're buying time on purpose, instead of leaking money out of habit.
scenes.caption: BUY TIME ON PURPOSE

scenes.text: Leak number twelve. Escalating vacations.

card.title: Vacations escalate
card.sub: every trip must top the last

scenes.caption: LEAK 12

scenes.text: With a raise, vacations often level up. A longer trip, a nicer hotel, a flight upgrade, a more distant destination. Travel can be one of the most rewarding things to spend money on. But many people put trips on credit cards and spend the next months paying them off.
scenes.caption: LEVEL UP TRAVEL

scenes.text: There's also a comparison trap. Each trip has to beat the last one, and the one you saw online. That escalation can turn a joyful habit into a big yearly expense, financed with debt.
scenes.caption: BEAT THE LAST TRIP

scenes.text: Try this: set up a travel sinking fund and pay for trips with cash you've already saved. Decide the budget before you plan, not after. You'll enjoy the trip more when there's no bill waiting at home.
scenes.caption: A TRAVEL FUND

scenes.text: Leak number thirteen. Kids' lifestyle creep.
scenes.caption: LEAK 13

scenes.text: Parents want the best for their kids, and a raise can make it feel possible. More activities, private lessons, travel sports, newer gear, bigger birthday parties. Each choice comes from love. But the costs can rise fast, and kids quickly adapt to the new normal, just like adults.
scenes.caption: OUT OF LOVE

scenes.text: The hard truth is that kids often value time and attention more than the most expensive version of every activity. And one of the biggest gifts you can give them is parents who aren't stressed about money, and a retirement that won't depend on them later.
scenes.caption: TIME OVER STUFF

scenes.text: Try this: let each child pick one or two activities they love, and set a yearly budget for them. Involve older kids in the decisions. It teaches them about trade offs, which might be one of the most valuable lessons of all.
scenes.caption: TEACH THE TRADE OFFS

scenes.text: Leak number fourteen. Gifts and social obligations.
scenes.caption: LEAK 14

scenes.text: When you earn more, people may expect more. Bigger wedding gifts, more expensive birthday presents, picking up the check more often, helping family members. Some of this is generous and beautiful. Some of it happens because you feel you should, not because you want to.
scenes.caption: EXPECTED GENEROSITY

scenes.text: Try this: decide your giving on purpose. Set a yearly budget for gifts and help, and plan for it in your sinking funds. Generosity is one of the best uses of money. Just make it a choice, not a pressure, so it doesn't quietly replace your own savings.
scenes.caption: GIVE ON PURPOSE

scenes.text: And remember, the most meaningful gifts are rarely the most expensive. A handwritten note, time together, a shared experience. People remember how you made them feel much more than what you spent.
scenes.caption: MEANING OVER PRICE

scenes.text: Leak number fifteen. Status brands.
scenes.caption: LEAK 15

scenes.text: With more income, it's tempting to signal success. Designer clothes, a luxury watch, a premium car badge. Economists have studied conspicuous consumption, spending meant to be seen, for over a century. Thorstein Veblen coined the term back in eighteen ninety nine.
scenes.caption: CONSPICUOUS CONSUMPTION

scenes.text: The trouble is that status spending is a race with no finish line. There's always a more expensive brand, and the people you're signaling to are usually too busy with their own lives to notice. Meanwhile, quiet wealth, the kind in investment accounts, is invisible but much more powerful.
scenes.caption: A RACE WITH NO FINISH

scenes.text: Try this: before buying a status item, ask who it's for. If it's genuinely for you, because you love the quality and will use it for years, fine. If it's for an audience, consider whether that audience is worth the money.
scenes.caption: WHO IS IT FOR?

scenes.text: Before the playbook, five signs you're on the lifestyle treadmill. One. You earn more than you did three years ago, but your savings balance is about the same. Two. You can't name where your last raise went. Three. Your fixed monthly costs have grown faster than your take home pay.
scenes.caption: SIGNS 1 TO 3

scenes.text: Four. You often think, I'd be fine if I just earned a little more. And five. Most of your upgrades in the last year were things you'd now struggle to undo, like a lease, a loan or a contract. If three or more of these feel familiar, you're not bad with money. You're normal. But normal is exactly what the playbook is designed to fix.
scenes.caption: SIGNS 4 AND 5

scenes.text: Quick pause. If you're counting your own leaks right now, you're not alone. Subscribe to the channel if this is helping. It's free, and it helps me keep making these videos for you. Now, the last five leaks, the ones that hurt your future most.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Angle three. The five leaks that hurt your long term wealth, and then the rule that stops them all.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Leak number sixteen. Not raising your retirement contributions.
scenes.caption: LEAK 16
scenes.short_hook: The raise rule that makes you rich instead of busy

scenes.text: Here's a quiet one. Many people set their retirement contribution once, as a percent of pay, and never touch it again. If it's a percent, it grows a little with a raise. But if it's a flat dollar amount, a raise does nothing for your future at all. All of the raise goes to today.
scenes.caption: SET ONCE, NEVER CHANGED

scenes.text: Many workplace plans offer an automatic increase feature, sometimes called auto escalation, that raises your contribution by one percent each year. It's one of the easiest ways to grow your savings without feeling it, because the increase usually comes with a raise.
scenes.caption: AUTO ESCALATION

scenes.text: Try this: log into your retirement plan today and check two things. Are you getting the full employer match? And is automatic increase turned on? If not, turn it on. It takes five minutes and could be worth tens of thousands of dollars over your career.
scenes.caption: FIVE MINUTES TODAY

scenes.text: Leak number seventeen. Higher credit limits.
scenes.caption: LEAK 17

scenes.text: When your income rises, card companies often raise your limits, and offer new cards. More available credit can make bigger purchases feel affordable, even if you don't have the cash. For people who pay in full, this doesn't matter much. For people who carry a balance, it can mean the debt grows with the income.
scenes.caption: MORE ROOM TO BORROW

scenes.text: Try this: treat your income, not your credit limit, as your spending ceiling. If you ever carry a balance, put the first part of every raise toward paying it off. Clearing high interest debt is like giving yourself a second raise.
scenes.caption: A SECOND RAISE

scenes.text: It's also worth checking how many cards you actually need. Every new card offer after a raise is designed to capture some of your new income. One or two cards, paid in full every month, cover almost everything most people need. More cards mostly mean more temptation and more due dates.
scenes.caption: ONE OR TWO IS ENOUGH

scenes.text: Leak number eighteen. Financing upgrades against future raises.
scenes.caption: LEAK 18

scenes.text: Some people spend a raise before they get it. They expect a promotion, so they buy the bigger house or the nicer car now, assuming the money will be there. But raises can be delayed, jobs can change, and companies can cut costs. Borrowing against future income turns a hope into an obligation.
scenes.caption: SPENDING THE FUTURE

scenes.text: Try this: only upgrade after the raise has actually arrived, and after it's been in your paycheck for at least a few months. If you can live without the upgrade during that time, you might find you don't need it at all.
scenes.caption: WAIT FOR THE MONEY

scenes.text: A useful habit is to live on last year's income for the first few months of a new raise. Bank the difference. If the raise turns out to be stable and you still want the upgrade, you'll be able to buy it with savings instead of a loan, which is a much stronger position.
scenes.caption: LIVE ON LAST YEAR'S INCOME

scenes.text: Leak number nineteen. Bonuses and windfalls with no plan.
scenes.caption: LEAK 19

scenes.text: Bonuses, tax refunds, commissions and gifts often arrive without a plan. And money without a plan tends to disappear into the general spending pool. Many people can't say, a month later, what happened to their last bonus.
scenes.caption: WHERE DID IT GO?

scenes.text: Try this: set a simple windfall rule before the money arrives. For example, half to long term goals like investing or debt, a quarter to a near term goal like a trip or a car fund, and a quarter for pure fun. You get to enjoy it, and you still make real progress.
scenes.caption: A WINDFALL RULE

scenes.text: And if the bonus is large, give yourself a cooling off period. Park it in a high yield savings account for thirty days before deciding anything. Big money decisions made in the excitement of a windfall are rarely the best ones. A month of patience costs nothing and often saves a lot.
scenes.caption: PARK IT FOR 30 DAYS

scenes.text: Leak number twenty. Locking in costs with contracts.
scenes.caption: LEAK 20

scenes.text: The most dangerous upgrades are the ones you can't easily undo. Long leases, car loans, mortgages, annual memberships, phone contracts, private school commitments. Once signed, they stay, even if your income drops. Lifestyle inflation becomes lifestyle lock in.
scenes.caption: LIFESTYLE LOCK IN

scenes.text: This is why many financial planners suggest keeping your fixed costs well below your income, so that if you lose a job or take a pay cut, you can still cover them. Flexibility is a form of wealth.
scenes.caption: FLEXIBILITY IS WEALTH

scenes.text: Try this: before signing any contract after a raise, ask, could I still pay this if my income went back to what it was last year? If the answer is no, you're betting the raise is permanent. Sometimes that's a good bet. Just make it on purpose.
scenes.caption: THE LAST YEAR TEST

scenes.text: So how do you enjoy a raise and still build wealth? Here's the simplest rule I know.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The fifty fifty raise rule. Every time your income goes up, send at least half of the increase to your future, and enjoy the other half guilt free.

card.label: the raise rule
card.sub: half to your future, half to enjoy

scenes.text: Here's how it works. Your take home pay goes up three hundred dollars a month. You immediately send one hundred fifty to investing, debt payoff or savings, ideally on autopay, before you ever see it. The other one hundred fifty is yours to enjoy. A nicer dinner, a hobby, a small upgrade. No guilt.
scenes.caption: HALF AND HALF

scenes.text: Why it works: you still feel the raise, so you don't feel deprived. But your savings rate goes up every single year. Over a career with many raises, that steady increase can build serious wealth, without ever feeling like a sacrifice.
scenes.caption: THE SAVINGS RATE CLIMBS

scenes.text: Investing an extra one hundred fifty dollars a month from one raise, at a seven percent average yearly return, for twenty five years. And that's just one raise.

And here's the magic. You'll probably get several raises over the next decade. If you apply the rule each time, the amounts stack. One hundred fifty, then three hundred, then four hundred fifty a month going to your future, while your lifestyle still improves every year. That's what getting richer actually looks like.
scenes.caption: THE RAISES STACK

scenes.text: Let's see lifestyle inflation at three income levels. Because it doesn't disappear when you earn more. It just gets more expensive.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: The same trap at three incomes

scenes.text: At fifty thousand dollars a year, the trap looks like this. A car payment that's a little too high, a few streaming services, takeout twice a week, and a credit card that's never quite paid off. The person feels like they'd be fine if they only earned a bit more.
scenes.caption: AT $50,000

scenes.text: At one hundred thousand, they do earn more. Now there's a bigger apartment or a starter home, two car payments in the household, a gym membership, more travel, and nicer restaurants. Savings are still small, because the new lifestyle costs almost exactly what the new income brings. They feel like they'd be fine if they only earned a bit more.
scenes.caption: AT $100,000

scenes.text: At two hundred thousand, the house is larger, the cars are luxury models, the kids are in expensive activities, and vacations are international. The numbers are bigger, but the feeling is the same. Tight. And notice the sentence they repeat. I'd be fine if I only earned a bit more. That sentence is the treadmill talking.
scenes.caption: AT $200,000

scenes.text: Now picture the same three people following the fifty fifty rule. At fifty thousand, they save a little. At one hundred thousand, they save a meaningful amount. At two hundred thousand, they can save a large share of their income and still live very comfortably. The income is the same in both versions. The difference is whether the raises went to the treadmill or to the future.
scenes.caption: SAME INCOME, DIFFERENT ENDINGS

scenes.text: If you're already deep in lifestyle creep, here's a thirty day reset. Four weeks, four steps.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Week one. Look. Download two months of statements and sort every expense into three groups. Needs, wants you love, and wants you barely notice. That third group is your target. Most people find a few hundred dollars a month there without cutting anything they truly care about.
scenes.caption: WEEK 1: LOOK

scenes.text: Week two. Cut the invisible. Cancel the subscriptions you don't use, call your phone, internet and insurance providers to lower your rates, and remove saved cards from shopping apps. These are one time actions that save money every month after.
scenes.caption: WEEK 2: CUT THE INVISIBLE

scenes.text: Week three. Automate the savings. Take the amount you freed up and set it to transfer automatically to savings or investing on payday. If the money disappears before you see it, you won't miss it. If it stays in checking, lifestyle creep will find it.
scenes.caption: WEEK 3: AUTOMATE

scenes.text: And week four. Decide the next raise. Write down, today, what you'll do with your next raise. Fifty fifty, or whatever split you choose. Turn on automatic increases in your retirement plan. That way, when the raise comes, the decision is already made, and the treadmill doesn't get a vote.
scenes.caption: WEEK 4: DECIDE THE NEXT RAISE

scenes.text: Let's look at two coworkers who got the same raises over ten years, from fifty thousand to eighty five thousand dollars a year. Ashley upgraded with every raise. A bigger apartment, a new car, more dinners out, nicer trips. At eighty five thousand, she had the same savings rate she had at fifty, close to zero, and still felt tight every month.
scenes.caption: ASHLEY: EVERY UPGRADE
scenes.short_hook: Two coworkers got the same raises. One got rich.

scenes.text: Ben followed the fifty fifty rule. With each raise, half went to his 401k and investments, and half to his life. His apartment got a bit nicer, he upgraded his car once, he traveled more. But his savings rate climbed from five percent to almost twenty percent of his pay over the decade.
scenes.caption: BEN: FIFTY FIFTY

scenes.text: After ten years, Ashley had a few thousand dollars saved. Ben had well over one hundred thousand dollars invested, depending on the market. Both enjoyed their lives. Both felt their income go up. But only one of them turned those raises into freedom.
scenes.caption: SAME RAISES, DIFFERENT FUTURES

scenes.text: And here's the part people miss. Ben didn't feel deprived. He felt every raise. He just felt half of each one. Ashley felt every raise fully, for a few months, and then it disappeared into her new normal. The treadmill took it.
scenes.caption: HE FELT EVERY RAISE

scenes.text: One more thing about Ben. Because his fixed costs stayed reasonable, he had options. When his company went through layoffs in year eight, he wasn't panicked. He had savings, a manageable rent and no car payment. He took his time, found a better job, and kept going. Ashley, with higher fixed costs, felt she had to stay in a job she didn't like, because she couldn't afford even a short gap in income. Lifestyle inflation doesn't just cost money. It costs choices.
scenes.caption: IT COSTS CHOICES

scenes.text: A few questions people ask me about lifestyle inflation.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Question one. Is all lifestyle inflation bad? No. Some upgrades genuinely improve your life, like a safer neighborhood, a shorter commute, better health care, or more time with family. The goal isn't to never upgrade. It's to upgrade on purpose, and make sure your savings grow too.
scenes.caption: IS ALL OF IT BAD?

scenes.text: Question two. What if I already inflated my lifestyle? Start with the leak that costs the most and adds the least joy. Often it's subscriptions, delivery, or a car payment. Undo one, and send that money to savings automatically. Then apply the fifty fifty rule to your next raise.
scenes.caption: ALREADY INFLATED?

scenes.text: Question three. What percent of income should I save? A common target for retirement is around fifteen percent of pre tax income, including any employer match, though it depends on your age and goals. If you're far from that, the raise rule is one of the most painless ways to get there.
scenes.caption: HOW MUCH TO SAVE?

scenes.text: Question four. My partner spends every raise. What do I do? Talk about goals before you talk about spending. What do you both want in five or ten years? Then agree on a simple rule, like fifty fifty, and automate it. It's easier to agree on a system than to argue about every purchase.
scenes.caption: MY PARTNER SPENDS IT

scenes.text: Question six. What if my raise is small, like two or three percent? Then the rule matters even more, because small raises are the easiest to lose without noticing. Even half of a small raise, sent to savings every year, adds up over a career. And small raises often roughly match inflation, so not spending them on upgrades keeps your budget from slipping backward.
scenes.caption: WHAT IF IT'S SMALL?

scenes.text: And question five. Does lifestyle inflation happen to rich people too? Absolutely. Many high earners, like doctors, lawyers and executives, struggle with it because their peer groups spend heavily. Income doesn't protect you from lifestyle inflation. A plan does.
scenes.caption: RICH PEOPLE TOO?

scenes.text: Before we wrap up, one honest note. Enjoying your money is part of the point. You worked for that raise. The goal of this video isn't to make you feel guilty about a nice dinner or a better apartment. It's to make sure that years from now, your raises added up to something you can see, not just a lifestyle you can't afford to leave.
scenes.caption: ENJOY IT, AND KEEP SOME

scenes.text: Quick recap. The money leaks: taxes, housing, cars, subscriptions, eating out, premium everything, and tech upgrades. The mind leaks: the hedonic treadmill, a new peer group, weekly treats, convenience spending, escalating vacations, kids' lifestyle creep, gifts and obligations, and status brands.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST 15

scenes.text: And the future leaks: not raising your contributions, higher credit limits, upgrades financed against future raises, bonuses with no plan, and locked in contracts. One rule stops them all. Half of every raise to your future. Half to enjoy.
scenes.caption: THE LAST 5 AND THE RULE

scenes.text: If you want the full plan for turning every raise into real wealth, it's in my playbook. The link is in the description. And watch my video on why most people stay broke. Lifestyle inflation is one of the biggest reasons. I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
